extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent counsel, judges, and parties in patent claim construction/Markman proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Court opinion applying §112 indefiniteness and means-plus-function legal standards to disputed patent claim terms (antecedent basis, "means"/"code for" language, algorithmic disclosure) in a Markman/claim-construction context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and burden of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall be presumed valid and the burden of establishing invalidity of a patent or any claim rests on the party asserting such invalidity. (35 U.S.C. § 282(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statements of invalidity (including indefiniteness) proceed under the presumption of validity. The opinion cites Sonix: 'Indefiniteness must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.' For specific showings (e.g., whether a particular phrase invokes §112, ¶6), the court references case law (Zeroclick) holding the party invoking that argument must carry the applicable burden (the opinion states the government has the burden of proving by a preponderance that 'code for' invokes §112, ¶6). Be explicit about which burden/standard applies to each asserted defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard — reasonable certainty to a skilled artisan
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is indefinite under §112, ¶2 if it fails to 'apprise a skilled artisan of the scope of the claimed invention with reasonable certainty.' (Nautilus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing indefiniteness, interpret claim language in light of the specification and prosecution history. Only 'reasonable certainty' is required; courts should determine whether a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would be reasonably certain of the claim's scope. If claims, read in light of the specification and prosecution history, fail to inform PHOSITA with reasonable certainty, find indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intrinsic evidence; do not construe claims in a vacuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim language is interpreted in light of all intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); claim terms are 'not construed in a vacuum.' (DeMarini; Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve ambiguities by reference to intrinsic record before turning to extrinsic evidence. Consider prior claim constructions in the case. Use the specification and prosecution history to inform meaning, but avoid importing limitations from embodiments without clear patentee intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import preferred embodiments into the claims absent express disavowal
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodiments in the specification are not to be read into the claims unless the patentee has expressly limited the claim to the embodiment. (Playtex; Karlin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a preferred embodiment shows particular structure or limitations, the court should not limit claim scope to that embodiment unless the patentee manifested an intent to limit. A party cannot create indefiniteness merely by pointing to a preferred embodiment and asking the court to read those details into the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis requirement (definite if PHOSITA can reasonably ascertain antecedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim phrasing like 'the [term]' must have antecedent basis in the independent claim; absence of explicit antecedent basis is not fatal if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by PHOSITA. (Energizer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple potential antecedents exist, resolve which antecedent PHOSITA would understand the dependent limitation to reference by reading the claims in context and against the specification. The court used this approach in deciding that 'the step of receiving' referred to the 'receiving a series of numerical values having tags...' clause rather than a macro-receiving clause because of language similarity and the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function framework under §112, ¶6
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may express an element as 'a means or step for performing a specified function' and, if so, the claim covers 'the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.' Presence of the word 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption of §112, ¶6 invocation, but the essential inquiry is whether the claim term names structure to PHOSITA. (35 U.S.C. §112, ¶6; Williamson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a claim term invokes §112, ¶6 by asking whether the words of the claim would be understood by PHOSITA as the name of structure. If §112, ¶6 applies, identify the corresponding structure in the specification (or equivalents); if no corresponding structure is disclosed, the claim is indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient structure requirement for means-plus-function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is not §112, ¶6 if the limitation recites sufficient structure; 'sufficient structure is recited if the claim term is used in common parlance or by persons of skill in the pertinent art to designate structure, even if the term covers a broad class of structures and even if the term identifies the structures by their function.' (Skky quoting TecSec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim term itself or known conventions would identify structure to PHOSITA. If the claim term (or its usage in the art) names structure, §112, ¶6 does not apply; if not, look to the specification for corresponding structure (including algorithmic detail for software).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-specific guidance: 'code for' is not automatically means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'code for' do not automatically invoke §112, ¶6; court should analyze whether 'code for' connotes sufficient structure to PHOSITA. (Zeroclick; Dyfan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party arguing 'code for' invokes §112, ¶6 bears the burden (court cites Zeroclick and states the government must prove by preponderance that 'code for' invokes §112, ¶6). Courts may look beyond the word 'code' to the functional language and the specification to determine whether PHOSITA would construe the limitation as connoting definite structure. Generic, term-by-term unsupported expert assertions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic disclosure requirement for software means-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For software-implemented functions claimed in means-plus-function format, the specification must disclose an algorithm (or other structure) corresponding to the claimed function to avoid indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a software limitation is treated as means-plus-function, identify algorithmic description(s) in the specification that map to the claimed function. If the specification contains algorithmic flowcharts, block diagrams with operations, or other specific disclosure enabling a PHOSITA to perform the function, the limitation may be definite; absence of such algorithmic structure supports a finding of indefiniteness (the court found Terms 3 and 4 supported by algorithmic disclosure but Terms 5–7 lacked disclosed structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat expert testimony cautiously and require term-by-term analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony must be consistent with the written patent record and provide reasoned, term-by-term analysis; courts may discount litigation-driven declarations or generic assertions that conflict with the intrinsic evidence. (Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts should explain, for each disputed term, how a PHOSITA would understand the term given the intrinsic evidence. Boilerplate or identical reasoning across many terms without supporting citation to the intrinsic record is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish indefiniteness from other §112 invalidity grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness (§112, ¶2) is analytically distinct from enablement and written description (other aspects of §112); arguments must be framed under the correct legal standard. (ePlus; Phillips; Process Control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate a lack of disclosed structure (an indefiniteness problem) with enablement or written-description defects; apply the correct standard and burden for each kind of §112 challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of well-established general knowledge in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The incorporation of general knowledge 'sufficiently well established in the art and referenced in the patent' can render a claim definite. (Presidio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification references concepts or structures that are well established in the art, courts may rely on that background knowledge to resolve claim scope and avoid indefiniteness, provided such general knowledge is properly referenced or relied upon in the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claim terms do not invoke §112, ¶6, apply plain and ordinary meaning consistent with intrinsic record
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disputed limitation is not governed by §112, ¶6 and is not indefinite, it is given its plain and ordinary meaning as understood by PHOSITA, consistent with prior claim constructions in the case. (Nautilus; Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt plain-and-ordinary-meaning constructions unless the intrinsic record requires a different construction. The court applied this to terms where it found no §112, ¶6 invocation (e.g., many 'code for' terms) and resolved antecedent-basis disputes by plain reading and specification context.
